mechanisms.statement: At T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 the cued base's wrong final answers are spread over many values (high answer-level entropy), while its right answers coincide. A plurality vote therefore picks the right value even when it is drawn in only 25-40 % of samples, and each added sample keeps resolving such problems until only near-zero-p problems remain. Long late answers (past 16k tokens) are also scattered when wrong, so finishing them adds right votes without creating wrong majorities.

mechanisms.statement: Vote gains come in parity steps. At even k many problems end in exact ties (36 of 500 at k=4) broken by the lowest sample index, i.e. by one random draw, so an even k adds little over the odd k before it, while an odd k breaks most 2-2 and 1-1-1-1 ties with one more draw. The curve over k is therefore a zigzag rising about 1.5 problems per odd step, with flat or slightly lower even steps.

mechanisms.statement: Under T 1.0 stopping is a sampled event: at each position the model draws a commit/stop token with a small hazard, so the cap-hit share is a survival probability. RL's top-8 directions add a near-constant logit to that hazard (cap hits 96, 77, 46, 25, 5 along the dial); dose multiplies it. Where the base fails by not stopping (short code tasks, fresh contests) the dial converts unfinished samples, at precision below the base's finished answers.

mechanisms.statement: A T 1.0 run is a set of independent per-problem Bernoulli draws: the run-to-run spread of a count is sqrt(sum p(1-p)), about 5-6 problems on MATH-500 and 6 on hard328 for these models, and the seed adds nothing systematic. A stored first sample is one such draw, so a 4-sample mean is 1/4 that draw plus 3/4 the model's mean, and adding one sample to a vote moves only the few problems it can flip.

mechanisms.statement: Long untruncated T 1.0 generations drift off-distribution (script switches into Chinese, restarted working) at a rate set by how far the prompt template is from the model's training format. Drifted continuations are almost never right (1 of 24 finish right). Think-SFT in its own ChatML <think> format samples a sharper, on-distribution next-token distribution, so fewer long answers drift, and its trained Answer line removes v3 undercounts; raw-template cue runs keep the drift.

mechanisms.statement: Adding RL-direction weight to a model concentrates its answer-level distribution: samples of one problem agree more, right or wrong. Higher dose therefore raises single-sample accuracy where answers are short but shrinks what a vote adds (vote/single 1.21 base, 1.07 for the 1.5x edit, 1.09 for Think-SFT + 2x on fresh2026). On short exact outputs such as code, concentration has no truncation cost, so code accuracy does not fall back at 2x as math did.
